title: Factory sensors
brief: A factory has thousands of machines, each sending readings many times a second. Engineers open charts of the last hour and last month, and an alarm must fire within seconds when a reading goes out of range. The data grows without end.

clarify.q: How quickly must an alarm fire?
clarify.a: Within 5 seconds of the bad reading.

clarify.q: How long do we keep full detail?
clarify.a: Five days in full. After that, one average per minute is enough for a year.
Yes. Readings wait on the machine and arrive later; late data must still be stored.

notes: Machines send readings throughout the day, without a quiet night.

Scored data retention: at least 5 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

hints: Data arrives non-stop and never goes away. What do you keep in full and what do you shrink?
A stream absorbs bursts and late data. A time-series database stores recent detail; old data moves to cheap storage.
An observability system must retain its deadline under expensive historical queries. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: A steady flood of small writes belongs in a stream and a database built for time. Alarms read the stream, so they do not wait for storage. Old detail is rolled up and moved to cheap object storage so cost stays flat as data grows.

designs.name: Stream, alarm processor and tiered storage
designs.why: The stream takes every reading and survives gaps. A processor checks limits within seconds, the time-series database holds the recent five days, and a nightly job moves older data to object storage as one-minute averages.

tradeoffs: Rolling up to one-minute averages cuts old data about 600 times, but you lose the short spikes.
A stream costs extra, but it lets alarms and storage work at their own pace and replay after a failure.
Compressing time-series data tightly saves disk, at the price of slower updates to old points.
Sending readings in small batches from the machine cuts request cost a lot.
editorial.realWorld: A busy plant can produce millions of readings a second. Teams keep days of detail on fast storage and months of averages on cheap storage (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Factory sensors: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Detect timely alarms from event-time data without letting history overwhelm ingestion. Duplicate uploads must not create duplicate alarms or biased aggregates. Watermarks and late-data policy distinguish historical anomalies from present conditions. An observability system must retain its deadline under expensive historical queries.

fields.label: Step 1. A sensor batch arrives twice. What updates the chart and alarm state?
options: Every arrival counts as a new measurement
fields.explanation: Duplicate uploads must not create duplicate alarms or biased aggregates.

fields.label: Step 2. An old out-of-range reading arrives after recovery. What alarm fires?
options: Apply an explicit event-time lateness policy and mark delayed evidence
Treat it as a current emergency solely by arrival time
fields.explanation: Watermarks and late-data policy distinguish historical anomalies from present conditions.

fields.label: Step 3. A month-wide query consumes all workers. What protects live alarms?
options: Separate query budgets and bounded scan concurrency from ingest and alert work
fields.explanation: An observability system must retain its deadline under expensive historical queries.

correctness.responsibility: Detect timely alarms from event-time data without letting history overwhelm ingestion.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 750 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $5,236. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
